evidence.claim: NY 97 follows the Delaware River corridor between Hancock and Port Jervis, with wooded stretches, river hamlets and tight curves above the water.
evidence.quote: Through Hancock, NY 97 becomes a two-lane woods road, winding north and soon northeast into the hamlet of Pea Brook.

evidence.claim: The Upper Delaware Scenic Byway joined the New York State Scenic Byways System on August 6, 2002.
evidence.quote: The Upper Delaware Scenic Byway was officially added to the New York State Scenic Byways System on August 6, 2002.

evidence.claim: Its byway organization highlights rolling hills, long vistas and rock formations along the 70-mile drive.
evidence.quote: The now, 70 mile stretch of 97 North encompasses rolling hills, long vistas and impressive rock formations.

evidence.claim: The legislature laid out a river route in 1911, but much of the highway still had to be built.
evidence.quote: The New York State Legislature created Route 3-a, an unsigned legislative route extending from Port Jervis to Hancock along the Delaware River, in 1911. Initially, it was a route in name only as the portion north of Port Jervis had yet to be built.

evidence.claim: Construction advanced during the 1920s; two sections remained unfinished when the NY 97 number was assigned in 1930.
evidence.quote: Several parts of the route were constructed during the 1920s, and by the time the NY 97 designation was created as part of the 1930 renumbering of state highways in New York, only two sections were still unconstructed.

evidence.claim: The whole highway opened on August 30, 1939, with a ribbon-cutting in Port Jervis and a motorcade along its length.
evidence.quote: On August 30, 1939, the entirety of NY 97 was officially opened to traffic. Several events were held to mark the road's opening, including a ribbon-cutting ceremony in Port Jervis featuring the mayors of Port Jervis and Hancock and a motorcade procession that traveled the length of the highway.

evidence.claim: Driving south from Hancock, the road winds through woods before reaching Long Eddy and Hankins.
evidence.quote: Through Hancock, NY 97 becomes a two-lane woods road, winding north and soon northeast into the hamlet of Pea Brook.

evidence.claim: Railroad tracks accompany it into Callicoon and through parts of Cochecton before Narrowsburg.
evidence.quote: In Delaware, NY 97 and the railroad tracks proceed northward, entering the hamlet of Callicoon.

evidence.claim: Farther south, Minisink Ford brings the crossing at Roebling's Delaware Aqueduct, followed by Barryville and Pond Eddy.
evidence.quote: NY 97 and CR 168 are concurrent for an extremely short distance, before CR 168 crosses the Delaware River on Roebling's Delaware Aqueduct into the borough of Lackawaxen, Pennsylvania.

evidence.claim: The Hawk's Nest carries the road along cliffs overlooking the Delaware before the final approach to Port Jervis.
evidence.quote: In Hawk's Nest, NY 97 runs alongside the side of several cliffs overlooking the Delaware.

evidence.claim: Callicoon was a transport center before it was a railroad depot: the Delaware carried lumber toward coastal cities to the south and east.
evidence.quote: the area was a source for lumber and a transport center with the Delaware River offering access to coastal cities to the south and east.

evidence.claim: In the 1840s, the Erie Railroad followed the riverbanks through the community, which took the name Callicoon Depot.
evidence.quote: In the 1840s, the Erie Railroad added to transportation by passing through along the banks of the Delaware River to link the Great Lakes with the East Coast. Because of the train station's vital central location, the community was renamed Callicoon Depot.

evidence.claim: A fire destroyed much of the business district in 1888, and rebuilding cost the town much of its earlier architecture.
evidence.quote: In 1888, a major fire destroyed much of Callicoon's business district. The town quickly rebuilt, but lost much of its architectural history prior to the late 19th century.

evidence.claim: The last scheduled passenger train left in 1966.
evidence.quote: The last scheduled passenger train left Callicoon on November 27, 1966.

evidence.claim: By the late 1960s, campgrounds and canoeing had helped tourism become the main industry.
evidence.quote: By the late 1960s, tourism took over as the main industry as campgrounds and canoes drew a new generation of visitors.

evidence.claim: Canal boats once crossed above the Delaware here at Minisink Ford.
evidence.quote: It runs 535 feet (163 meters) over the Delaware River, from Minisink Ford, New York, to Lackawaxen, Pennsylvania. Opened in 1849 as an aqueduct connecting two parts of the Delaware & Hudson Canal (D&H)

evidence.claim: The canal ferry had created a bottleneck and collisions with timber rafts heading downstream.
evidence.quote: The D&H Canal's rope ferry crossing of the Delaware at Lackawaxen created a bottleneck, and there were numerous collisions with timber rafts headed downstream.

evidence.claim: Russell F. Lord and John A. Roebling designed the replacement aqueduct, which opened in 1849.
evidence.quote: Russell F. Lord and John A. Roebling designed the bridge and supervised its construction.

evidence.claim: After the canal closed in 1898, the aqueduct was drained and converted for vehicles.
evidence.quote: After the canal closed in 1898, the aqueduct was drained and converted into a vehicular bridge.

evidence.claim: It is the oldest existing wire suspension bridge in the United States, but its canal appearance includes later reconstruction.
evidence.quote: is the oldest existing wire suspension bridge in the United States.

evidence.claim: The National Park Service rebuilt the superstructure in 1986 and reconstructed the towpaths, aqueduct walls and wooden icebreakers in 1995.
evidence.quote: The agency rebuilt the bridge's superstructure from Roebling's original plans and specification in 1986, and in 1995, the wooden icebreakers, towpaths and aqueduct walls were reconstructed

evidence.claim: The tight bends of the Hawk's Nest run along cliffs above the Delaware, a few miles north of Port Jervis.
evidence.quote: Its most famous feature is the Hawk's Nest, a tightly winding section of the road along the Delaware River, located a few miles north of Port Jervis.

evidence.claim: Early plans for the improved highway would have taken it along the shoreline instead.
evidence.quote: When the plans for a new highway through the corridor of NY 97 were initially drawn up, it was to bypass what became the Hawk's Nest in favor of a shoreline route.

evidence.claim: The Erie Railroad refused to sell the necessary right-of-way, so the state built along the cliffside.
evidence.quote: However, the Erie Railroad refused to sell the necessary right-of-way, forcing the state to construct the improved road along the cliffside instead.

evidence.claim: This section cost $2 million of the $4 million spent on NY 97.
evidence.quote: The portion through the Hawk's Nest cost $2 million

evidence.claim: The winding road has overlooks into the Delaware River Valley.
evidence.quote: The location is also known for its winding roads and scenic overlooks in the Delaware River Valley.

evidence.claim: The road bends along cliffs overlooking the Delaware.
evidence.quote: In Hawk's Nest, NY 97 runs alongside the side of several cliffs overlooking the Delaware.

evidence.claim: $4 million spent on NY 97
evidence.quote: In all, it cost $4 million

evidence.claim: The Route Ninety-Seven Council campaigned to give the entire road one number, opposing a proposed NY 17L designation; the state chose NY 97 in June 1939.
evidence.quote: The Route Ninety-Seven Council had been created several months prior to advocate for designating the entire road as NY 97. They opposed the decision for NY 17L, preferring to keep NY 97 to help travelers.

evidence.claim: the state chose NY 97 in June 1939
evidence.quote: On June 28, the state announced that they were dropping the NY 17L designation and the entire route would be designated as NY 97.

evidence.claim: Downtown became the Callicoon Downtown Historic District, added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2016.
evidence.quote: Downtown Callicoon is part of the Callicoon Downtown Historic District, which was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2016.

evidence.claim: A cliffside road had linked this river corridor since at least 1851, before the modern highway’s construction.
evidence.quote: The Delaware River corridor had been linked by a road along the cliffs overlooking the river since at least 1851.

flags: The route article describes a 1932 naming law; the byway organization dates entry into the state scenic-byways system to 2002. The story uses the latter for program designation.
Bridge history and reconstructed features are supported by secondary cache material; no site-manager page verifies current access, so no access promise is made.
